united-arab-republic.t: The union of Egypt and Syria under Gamal Abdel Nasser, the high point of pan-Arab nationalism.
united-arab-republic.o: Syrian officers and Ba'athist politicians, alarmed by communist influence and inspired by Nasser's prestige after the 1956 Suez crisis, asked Egypt for union. On 1 February 1958 the United Arab Republic was proclaimed, with Nasser as president and Cairo as capital; a plebiscite confirmed it.
united-arab-republic.r: Syria became the northern region of a centralised state. Political parties were dissolved, including the Ba'ath, and Egyptian officials and security services dominated, with Field Marshal Abdel Hakim Amer as Nasser's representative in Damascus. Land reform and the nationalisation of banks and industry in 1961 alienated Syrian landowners and merchants. A loose confederation with North Yemen, the United Arab States, was also formed.
united-arab-republic.e: On 28 September 1961 Syrian officers seized power in Damascus and declared secession. Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic until 1971.

urusalim.t: Urusalim, the Canaanite city-state of Jerusalem, a small Egyptian vassal in the Amarna age that later became the capital of King David.
urusalim.o: Jerusalem grew around the Gihon spring on a ridge in the Judaean hills. Egyptian execration texts of the 19th century BCE mention Rushalimum, and in the Middle Bronze Age its inhabitants built massive towers to protect the spring.
urusalim.r: In the 14th century BCE its ruler Abdi-Heba, a vassal of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, wrote several Amarna letters complaining about rivals such as Shechem and asking for troops. The Bible calls the later inhabitants Jebusites and the city Jebus. Its realm was a modest hill country territory.
urusalim.e: According to the Bible, David captured the city c. 1000 BCE and made it the capital of the United Kingdom of Israel. The Canaanite city thus became the centre of later Jewish, Christian and Islamic history.

united-provinces-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.t: The revolutionary state formed in Buenos Aires in 1810 that declared independence from Spain in 1816 and became the core of Argentina.
united-provinces-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.o: The May Revolution of 25 May 1810 replaced the viceroy of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata with a Primera Junta in Buenos Aires. Armies were sent to spread the revolution, but Paraguay and Upper Peru resisted, and Montevideo held out for Spain until 1814.
united-provinces-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.r: Government passed from juntas to triumvirates and, from 1814, Supreme Directors. Manuel Belgrano created the blue and white flag in 1812, and the Assembly of the Year XIII abolished titles and freed children born to enslaved mothers. The Congress of Tucumán declared independence on 9 July 1816. José de San Martín's Army of the Andes liberated Chile in 1817 and 1818. Conflict between Buenos Aires and federalist provinces, such as those of the Federal League, was constant.
united-provinces-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.e: After the Battle of Cepeda in 1820 central government collapsed. Bernardino Rivadavia's presidency and a war with Brazil over Cisplatina followed. The Federal Pact of 1831 created the Argentine Confederation.

ukrainian-peoples-republic.t: The Ukrainian national republic born in the Russian Revolution, which declared independence in 1918 and fought for its survival until 1921.
ukrainian-peoples-republic.o: In March 1917 Ukrainian parties formed the Central Rada in Kyiv, chaired by the historian Mykhailo Hrushevsky. After the October Revolution its Third Universal of November 1917 proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic, and the Fourth Universal of January 1918 declared full independence.
ukrainian-peoples-republic.r: The Rada passed land reform and made a separate peace with the Central Powers at Brest-Litovsk in February 1918, relying on German troops against the Bolsheviks. In April 1918 the Germans replaced it with the Ukrainian State, but in December a Directorate led by Volodymyr Vynnychenko and Symon Petliura restored the republic. In January 1919 it proclaimed union with the West Ukrainian People's Republic.
ukrainian-peoples-republic.e: Attacked by Bolsheviks, Whites and Poles, the republic lost most of its territory in 1919. Petliura allied with the Second Polish Republic in 1920, but the Peace of Riga in 1921 divided Ukraine between Poland and the Ukrainian SSR. The government continued in exile until 1992.

ursum.t: Ursum, a north Syrian city on the caravan routes to Anatolia, remembered for its long siege by the Hittite king Hattusili I.
ursum.o: Urshu lay west of the Euphrates, probably near modern Gaziantep, on the routes between Syria and Anatolia. It appears in Old Assyrian trade letters and the Mari archives as a city with its own king, a place where merchants traded and a temple of the god Ea was honoured.
ursum.r: Little is known of its government. The Mari letters show it linked to the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia and Yamhad in the politics of the 18th century BCE.
ursum.e: In the 17th century BCE Hattusili I of the Hittite Empire besieged Ursum for months. A Hittite literary text, the Siege of Urshu, mocks his generals' failures. The city fell and lost its independence.

united-baltic-duchy.t: Short-lived German client state proclaimed by Baltic German nobles in late 1918, meant to unite Estonia and Livonia under a German duke.
united-baltic-duchy.o: During the German occupation of 1918, Baltic German nobles sought to keep their dominance. Councils dominated by them asked for a union with Germany, and on 5 November 1918 a United Baltic Duchy was proclaimed in Riga, covering the former Governorate of Estonia and Governorate of Livonia, with the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia (1918) to join.
united-baltic-duchy.r: Duke Adolf Friedrich of Mecklenburg was chosen as head of state but never took office. A regency council under Baron Adolf Pilar von Pilchau governed in name only, relying entirely on German troops. Latvians and Estonians, who were the great majority of the population, rejected the state.
united-baltic-duchy.e: Germany's defeat in the First World War doomed the duchy. The regency council dissolved itself on 28 November 1918, and its territory passed to the Republic of Estonia and the Republic of Latvia, amid fighting with Soviet forces. Baltic German volunteers later fought in the Landeswehr.

united-kingdom-of-portugal-brazil-and-th.t: A transatlantic monarchy ruled from Rio de Janeiro, created when Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal to Portugal in 1815.
united-kingdom-of-portugal-brazil-and-th.o: Fleeing Napoleon's invasion, the Portuguese court sailed to Brazil in 1807-1808 and settled in Rio de Janeiro. On 16 December 1815 the Prince Regent John raised Brazil from colony to the Kingdom of Brazil, uniting it with the Kingdom of Portugal and the Kingdom of the Algarve.
united-kingdom-of-portugal-brazil-and-th.r: Rio became the seat of government of a global empire, with new ministries, a royal library, a bank and opened ports. John VI, acclaimed king in 1818 after the death of Maria I, stayed in Brazil, while Portugal was governed by a regency under strong British influence and resented its subordinate status.
united-kingdom-of-portugal-brazil-and-th.e: The Liberal Revolution in Porto in 1820 forced John VI to return to Lisbon in 1821, leaving his son Pedro as regent. When the Lisbon Cortes tried to reduce Brazil's status, Pedro declared independence on 7 September 1822, founding the Brazilian Empire.

united-provinces-of-central-italy.t: A short-lived union of Tuscany, Modena, Parma and Romagna formed in 1859, which voted to join Piedmont and paved the way for Italian unity.
united-provinces-of-central-italy.o: During the war of 1859 between Austria and the alliance of France and the Kingdom of Sardinia, the rulers of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the Duchy of Modena and Reggio and the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza fled, and the papal Legations of Romagna rebelled. Their provisional governments formed a league with a common army under General Manfredo Fanti.
united-provinces-of-central-italy.r: The union was a military and political alliance rather than a full state. Luigi Carlo Farini governed Modena, Parma and Romagna, united as Emilia, while Bettino Ricasoli led Tuscany. Their assemblies voted to join the Kingdom of Sardinia, defying the Peace of Villafranca, which had foreseen the return of the old rulers.
united-provinces-of-central-italy.e: After plebiscites in March 1860, the territories were annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia, with France receiving Nice and Savoy in exchange. They became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

usfurid-dynasty.t: A Bedouin dynasty of the Banu Uqayl that replaced the Uyunids in eastern Arabia and controlled the al-Ahsa oasis in the 13th and 14th centuries.
usfurid-dynasty.o: The Usfurids, named after their ancestor Usfur ibn Rashid, were a clan of the Banu Amir branch of the Banu Uqayl tribe. Around 1253 they took al-Ahsa from the weakened Uyunid Emirate and became the leading power of eastern Arabia.
usfurid-dynasty.r: Their power rested on Bedouin tribal forces and on the revenues of the date oases and the pilgrimage and trade routes between Iraq and the Hejaz. They maintained links with the Ilkhanate in Iraq and Iran and competed with the Kingdom of Ormus for control of the Bahrain islands and the Gulf ports. Sources on them are thin.
usfurid-dynasty.e: In the early 14th century the Usfurids lost the islands and Qatif to rulers allied with Hormuz, and by about 1330 their authority had passed to the Jarwanid dynasty and other local leaders.

urkesh.t: Urkesh, a Hurrian city-kingdom in north-eastern Syria, revered in myth as the home of the god Kumarbi and ruled by kings with the title endan.
urkesh.o: Urkesh grew at Tell Mozan in the foothills of the Taurus mountains, controlling access to the copper of the Anatolian highlands. By the mid-3rd millennium BCE it was the main political and religious centre of the Hurrians, a people who spoke a language unrelated to the Semitic tongues of their neighbours.
urkesh.r: Its rulers bore the Hurrian title endan. Excavations led by Giorgio and Marilyn Buccellati since 1984 uncovered the palace of King Tupkish and Queen Uqnitum, a great temple terrace and a deep ritual pit used to summon underworld spirits. A daughter of Naram-Sin of the Akkadian Empire, Tar'am-Agade, lived there, probably as a royal bride.
urkesh.e: Urkesh lost importance in the early 2nd millennium BCE, appearing in the Mari letters as a minor kingdom. It survived as a religious centre under the Mitanni Empire before being largely abandoned in the 14th century BCE, though Hurrian myths kept its name alive.

uzbek-khanate.t: The nomadic khanate of Abu'l-Khayr Khan on the Kazakh steppe, from which both the Uzbek dynasties of Transoxiana and the Kazakhs emerged.
uzbek-khanate.o: In 1428 the Shibanid prince Abu'l-Khayr was proclaimed khan in western Siberia by the tribes of the former Ulus of Shiban and White Horde. He conquered the steppe as far as the Syr Darya and in 1446 took Sighnaq and other Syr Darya towns, making them his base.
uzbek-khanate.r: Abu'l-Khayr ruled a confederation of Turkic tribes, including the Qungrat, Mangit and Kiyat, known collectively as Uzbeks. He intervened in Timurid politics, sacking Urgench in 1431 and backing the Timurid Abu Sa'id. In 1457 his army was badly defeated by the Kalmyks (Oirats), and discontented clans under Kerei and Janibek broke away to form the Kazakh Khanate.
uzbek-khanate.e: Abu'l-Khayr died in 1468 and his state collapsed amid rival claims, its tribes passing largely to the Kazakhs. His grandson Muhammad Shaybani regrouped the Uzbeks and in 1500 conquered Transoxiana, founding the Khanate of Bukhara.

ustrushana.t: A mountain principality between Samarkand and Ferghana whose Afshin rulers rose to command the armies of the Abbasid caliphate.
ustrushana.o: Ustrushana lay along the upper Syr Darya and the Turkestan range, around the town of Bunjikat near modern Istaravshan. Its rulers, who bore the title afshin, emerged in the 7th century as Sogdian-speaking lords in the zone of the Western Turkic Khaganate.
ustrushana.r: Excavations at Bunjikat and Shahristan revealed palaces with wall paintings, including an image of a she-wolf suckling twins. The afshins long resisted Arab conquest, submitting to the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun only around 822. The afshin Khaydhar ibn Kawus became a top general for al-Mu'tasim, crushing the revolt of Babak Khorramdin, before being tried for heresy and dying in prison in 841.
ustrushana.e: The afshins continued as local governors under Abbasid and Samanid authority until 893, when the Samanid Empire's Isma'il ibn Ahmad ended their dynasty and absorbed Ustrushana.

upper-aulaqi-sheikhdom.t: A small tribal sheikhdom of the Aulaqi people, separate from the neighbouring Aulaqi sultanates, in the hinterland of British Aden.
upper-aulaqi-sheikhdom.o: The Aulaqi tribes of the Shabwa region were divided among several rulers. The Upper Aulaqi Sheikhdom, with its seat at Said, emerged as a distinct polity by around 1800, alongside the Upper Aulaqi Sultanate and the Lower Aulaqi Sultanate.
upper-aulaqi-sheikhdom.r: Its sheikhs ruled by tribal custom over a mountainous and semi-desert district. Like its neighbours it signed protection treaties with Britain and became part of the Aden Protectorate. In 1959 it was one of the six founding members of the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South. Little else is recorded of its internal history.
upper-aulaqi-sheikhdom.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over the region and the sheikhdom was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

ugandi.t: Ancient Estonian county of the south-east, centred on the hillforts of Otepää and Tartu, which fought Rus' and the German crusaders before falling in 1224.
ugandi.o: Ugandi, in what is now south-eastern Estonia, was one of the larger Estonian lands of the late Iron Age, a union of parishes defended by hillforts. Its position on routes to Pskov and Novgorod drew Rus' attention early: Yaroslav the Wise of Kiev captured Tartu around 1030 and briefly held it as Yuryev.
ugandi.r: Ugandi was governed by elders of its districts, who met to decide on war and tribute. Its people grew grain, kept cattle and traded with Rus' and the Latgalians to the south. Otepää, whose name means 'bear's head', was its main stronghold, and Tartu on the Emajõgi river guarded the waterway east to Lake Peipus.
ugandi.e: From 1208 the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and their Latgalian allies raided Ugandi, and Otepää changed hands several times. When Tartu fell in 1224, after a siege in which the Rus' prince Vyachko was killed, the conquest was complete. Ugandi became the core of the Bishopric of Dorpat.

united-states-of-colombia.t: A radically federal Colombian republic of nine sovereign states, created by the Liberals in 1863 and ended by the centralist constitution of 1886.
united-states-of-colombia.o: After winning the civil war of 1860 to 1862 against the Granadine Confederation, Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera and the Liberals met at Rionegro in Antioquia and adopted a new constitution in 1863, creating the United States of Colombia, made up of nine sovereign states including Panama.
united-states-of-colombia.r: The Rionegro constitution gave the states their own armies and laws, limited the president to a two-year term and guaranteed broad freedoms, including freedom of the press and of trade in arms. The Radical Liberals separated church and state and promoted secular public schools. The weak central government struggled with frequent regional civil wars, notably the church-backed war of 1876 and 1877.
united-states-of-colombia.e: Rafael Núñez led a movement called the Regeneration. After the civil war of 1885, the constitution of 1886 restored a centralised Republic of Colombia with strong ties to the Catholic Church.

ulus-of-shiban.t: The appanage of Jochi's son Shiban in western Siberia and the southern Urals, from which the Shaybanid dynasties of Bukhara and Khiva descended.
ulus-of-shiban.o: Shiban, a son of Jochi, distinguished himself in Batu's western campaign of the late 1230s. In reward he received pastures east of the Urals, in the region of the Tobol, Tura and Irtysh, as an appanage within the Golden Horde.
ulus-of-shiban.r: The Shibanids ruled nomadic Kipchak and Mongol tribes and Siberian forest peoples, collecting furs, with Chimgi-Tura (later Tyumen) as a seat. They acted as junior members of the Jochid house, taking part in the Golden Horde's politics and civil wars in the 14th century, when several Shibanid princes claimed the throne at Sarai.
ulus-of-shiban.e: As the Golden Horde collapsed, the Shibanid Abu'l-Khayr Khan proclaimed himself khan in 1428, founding the Uzbek Khanate. Other Shibanids founded the Tyumen Khanate. Abu'l-Khayr's grandson Muhammad Shaybani later conquered Transoxiana, establishing the Khanate of Bukhara.

utica.t: One of the oldest Phoenician cities in North Africa, an ally and rival of Carthage that later became Rome's first African capital.
utica.o: Utica stood at the mouth of the Bagradas (Medjerda) river, north-west of Carthage. Ancient writers such as Pliny the Elder dated its foundation by Phoenicians from Tyre to 1101 BCE, making it older than Carthage. Archaeology has so far found remains only from about the 8th century BCE, so the traditional date is debated.
utica.r: Utica was a self-governing Punic city with its own magistrates (suffetes) and harbour, trading in grain, olive oil and fish. It became an ally of Carthage and part of the Punic Empire but often kept its distance, joining the rebels in the Mercenary War of 240 to 238 BCE. Its gods were the Phoenician Baal and Tanit.
utica.e: In the Third Punic War Utica sided with Rome, which made it a free city and the capital of the new province of Africa. Cato the Younger killed himself there in 46 BCE after Caesar's victory at Thapsus, and the city merged into Africa Proconsularis. The silting of the Medjerda later left its ruins inland.

united-principalities.t: Union of Moldavia and Wallachia under one prince that created the modern Romanian state and won its independence from the Ottomans.
united-principalities.o: After the Crimean War the Paris settlement allowed Moldavia and Wallachia separate assemblies under a common commission. Exploiting a loophole, both assemblies elected the same man, Alexandru Ioan Cuza, as prince in January and February 1859. The personal union became a single state with one government and parliament in Bucharest in 1862, taking the name Romania.
united-principalities.r: Cuza secularised the vast monastery estates in 1863, carried out a land reform in 1864, introduced a civil code and founded the universities of Iași and Bucharest. His authoritarian methods provoked a coup in 1866, and Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was installed as prince under a liberal constitution modelled on Belgium's. Grain exports through Galați and Brăila drove the economy.
united-principalities.e: Romania declared independence in 1877 and fought alongside Russia against the Ottomans. The Congress of Berlin in 1878 recognised independence, adding Northern Dobruja but returning southern Bessarabia to Russia. In 1881 Carol was crowned king, founding the Kingdom of Romania.

ubykhia.t: The land of the Ubykhs around Sochi, a small Black Sea people who led the last Circassian resistance and whose language died out in 1992.
ubykhia.o: The Ubykhs lived on the Black Sea coast and mountain valleys around modern Sochi, between the Shapsugs and the Abkhaz. They spoke a distinct Northwest Caucasian language with a famously large number of consonants. They are recorded as a separate people by the 17th century; earlier history is little known.
ubykhia.r: Ubykh society was led by noble families, above all the Berzeg, together with free communities, and lived by farming, herding and sea trade with Ottoman ports. In 1861 the Ubykhs hosted the Circassian assembly at Sochi, led by Haji Kerantukh Berzeg, which appealed to Britain and the Ottomans for help against Russia.
ubykhia.e: The Russian Empire overran Ubykhia in 1864, and the entire Ubykh people were expelled to the Ottoman Empire. Their language faded in exile; its last fluent speaker, Tevfik Esenc, died in Turkey in 1992.

upper-palatinate.t: The Wittelsbach iron country north of the Danube, ruled from Amberg for the Electors Palatine until Bavaria seized it in the Thirty Years' War.
upper-palatinate.o: By the Treaty of Pavia in 1329, Emperor Louis the Bavarian divided the Wittelsbach possessions, giving the Rhineland Palatinate and the northern part of the Bavarian Nordgau to his nephews. This upland region between Regensburg and the Bohemian border, ruled from Amberg, became known as the Upper Palatinate, an outlying part of the Electoral Palatinate.
upper-palatinate.r: A governor in Amberg ran the land for the electors in Heidelberg; from 1595 this was Christian of Anhalt, architect of Protestant policy. The region's wealth came from iron mining and smelting around Amberg and Sulzbach, which made it the Ruhr of the Middle Ages. Its people were obliged to follow their rulers through Lutheranism and Calvinism, often against the wishes of the estates.
upper-palatinate.e: After Elector Frederick V's defeat at the White Mountain in 1620, Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria occupied the Upper Palatinate and in 1628 annexed it, re-Catholicising the population. The Peace of Westphalia confirmed it as part of the Electorate of Bavaria.

united-kingdom.t: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, the state that emerged from Irish partition in 1922 and has remained a leading European power.
united-kingdom.o: When the Irish Free State left in December 1922, the remaining state continued as the United Kingdom, formally renamed the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland in 1927. It still ruled a large empire and was a major power after the First World War.
united-kingdom.r: The UK is a constitutional monarchy with a Parliament at Westminster, uncodified constitution and common law in England and Wales, with separate Scots law. It fought the Second World War under Churchill, created the National Health Service and welfare state after 1945, and decolonised its empire. Devolution in 1999 created parliaments or assemblies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
united-kingdom.e: The UK joined the European Economic Community in 1973 and left the European Union in 2020 after the 2016 referendum. It remains a permanent member of the UN Security Council and a nuclear power.
united-kingdom.re: Christianity; Church of England, Church of Scotland

united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.t: The state formed by uniting Great Britain and Ireland in 1801, centre of the largest empire in history and of the industrial world.
united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.o: After the 1798 rebellion in Ireland, the Acts of Union of 1800, passed by both Parliaments, abolished the Irish Parliament and merged the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland into one state from 1 January 1801, with Irish members sitting at Westminster.
united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.r: The United Kingdom defeated Napoleon, led the Industrial Revolution and built a global empire. Parliamentary reform from 1832, Catholic Emancipation in 1829 and Queen Victoria's long reign shaped the century. The Great Famine of 1845 to 1852 killed about a million in Ireland and caused mass emigration, and Irish Home Rule became a central political issue.
united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel.e: After the First World War, the Easter Rising and the Irish War of Independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921 created the Irish Free State in 1922. The rest became the United Kingdom, renamed in 1927.

unitarian-league.t: An alliance of nine Argentine interior provinces under General José María Paz, defeated by the federalists in 1831.
unitarian-league.o: During the civil wars between Unitarians, who wanted a centralised Argentina, and Federalists, General José María Paz took control of Córdoba in 1829. He defeated the federal caudillo Juan Facundo Quiroga at La Tablada in 1829 and Oncativo in 1830, and in 1830 the interior provinces formed the League of the Interior with Paz as Supreme Military Chief.
unitarian-league.r: The league joined nine provinces, including Córdoba, Tucumán, Salta, Mendoza and San Juan, under Unitarian governors installed with Paz's backing. It was mainly a military alliance. In response, Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Entre Ríos signed the Federal Pact in January 1831.
unitarian-league.e: In May 1831 Paz was captured when soldiers of Estanislao López lassoed his horse. Quiroga defeated the Unitarians at La Ciudadela near Tucumán in November 1831, and the provinces joined the Federal Pact, forming the Argentine Confederation.

ukrainian-peoples-republic-of-soviets.t: The first Soviet government in Ukraine, set up by Bolsheviks in Kharkiv as a rival to the Central Rada in Kiev.
ukrainian-peoples-republic-of-soviets.o: In December 1917, after Bolshevik delegates walked out of a congress of soviets in Kiev dominated by supporters of the Central Rada, they held their own congress in Kharkiv. It proclaimed Ukraine a republic of soviets in federation with Soviet Russia, in opposition to the Ukrainian People's Republic.
ukrainian-peoples-republic-of-soviets.r: The government, called the People's Secretariat, included Yevhenia Bosh, Mykola Skrypnyk and Volodymyr Zatonsky. It depended heavily on Red Guards sent from Russia, which under Mikhail Muravyov captured Kiev in February 1918 and carried out mass killings there. Its authority was weak, and several other Soviet republics existed alongside it in eastern and southern Ukraine.
ukrainian-peoples-republic-of-soviets.e: After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, German and Austro-Hungarian troops drove the Bolsheviks out of Ukraine. In March 1918 the republic merged with the other Soviet republics into the Ukrainian Soviet Republic, which was dissolved in April as its leaders withdrew to Russia.

uzbek-ssr.t: The Soviet republic of the Uzbeks, Central Asia's most populous, whose cotton monoculture shaped its economy and drained the Aral Sea.
uzbek-ssr.o: The Uzbek SSR was formed in October 1924 in the national delimitation of Soviet Central Asia, from parts of the Turkestan ASSR and the Bukharan and Khorezm republics. Its first capital was Samarkand; Tashkent became the capital in 1930. The Tajik ASSR was part of it until 1929, and Karakalpakstan joined in 1936.
uzbek-ssr.r: The republic was transformed by collectivisation, the Latin and then Cyrillic scripts, the hujum campaign against veiling, and purges that killed leaders like Fayzulla Khodzhayev and Akmal Ikramov. Cotton became the central crop, irrigated from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, causing the Aral Sea to shrink. Under Sharof Rashidov, first secretary from 1959 to 1983, the 'cotton scandal' exposed massive fraud. Tashkent was rebuilt after the earthquake of 1966.
uzbek-ssr.e: As the Soviet Union collapsed, Islam Karimov's government declared independence on 31 August 1991, and the republic became Uzbekistan.

ural-cossack-host.t: A self-governing Cossack community on the Ural River, guardians of Russia's steppe frontier and the starting point of Pugachev's great rebellion.
ural-cossack-host.o: Cossacks, many from the Don, settled on the Yaik River, later renamed the Ural, in the late 16th century, establishing a fishing and raiding community. In 1591 they took part in a Russian campaign, and the host is traditionally dated to that year. Their main town, Yaitsky Gorodok, later became Uralsk.
ural-cossack-host.r: The host was governed by an elected ataman and an assembly, the krug, and lived by fishing for sturgeon and caviar on the river, held in common, and by military service. Many were Old Believers. As the Russian state tightened control, discontent grew; in 1772 a revolt broke out, and in 1773 Yaik Cossacks backed Yemelyan Pugachev's rebellion against Catherine the Great.
ural-cossack-host.e: After the revolt, Catherine renamed the Yaik the Ural and the host the Ural Cossack Host. It served Russia in Central Asian campaigns. During the Russian Civil War the Ural Cossacks fought the Bolsheviks, and the host was destroyed in 1920.

ui-fidgenti.t: Kingdom of west County Limerick whose king Donnubán sided with the Vikings of Limerick against Brian Bóruma, and from whom the O'Donovans descend.
ui-fidgenti.o: The Uí Fidgenti claimed descent from Fiachu Fidgenid, a kinsman of the Eóganachta, and held much of what is now County Limerick west of the Maigue from the early medieval period. They formed a subject but partly privileged kingdom within the Kingdom of Munster, divided into branches such as the Uí Chonaill Gabra.
ui-fidgenti.r: The kingdom rested on cattle and the fertile lands south of the Shannon. In the 10th century it was caught between the rising Dál Cais of Thomond and the Norse town of Limerick. Its king Donnubán mac Cathail allied with Ivar of Limerick and helped bring about the death of Mathgamain, brother of Brian Bóruma, in 976, which drew Brian's revenge.
ui-fidgenti.e: After Brian's victories the Uí Fidgenti were reduced, and in the late 12th century the Anglo-Norman advance into Limerick, especially by the FitzGeralds, displaced them. Donnubán's descendants, the O'Donovans, moved south into Cork, where they held lordships near Skibbereen for centuries.

united-kingdom-of-israel.t: The United Monarchy of Saul, David and Solomon, remembered in the Bible as Israel's golden age, whose scale historians still debate.
united-kingdom-of-israel.o: According to the Hebrew Bible, the Israelite tribes, pressed by the Philistine Pentapolis, made Saul their king in the late 11th century BCE. David then united Israel and Judah, captured Urusalim and made Jerusalem his capital.
united-kingdom-of-israel.r: The Bible describes David's conquests of Moab, Ammon, Edom and Aram-Zobah, and Solomon's temple, palace and trade with Hiram I of Tyre. Archaeology confirms a dynasty called the House of David in the 9th-century Tel Dan stele, but the size and wealth of the kingdom are much debated. Yahweh was the national god.
united-kingdom-of-israel.e: After Solomon's death c. 930 BCE, the northern tribes rejected his son Rehoboam and made Jeroboam king, splitting the realm into the Kingdom of Israel and the Kingdom of Judah. The memory of the united monarchy shaped Jewish and later messianic hopes.

ukrainian-state.t: Hetman Pavlo Skoropadsky's conservative Ukrainian monarchy of 1918, installed with German backing, which founded Ukraine's Academy of Sciences.
ukrainian-state.o: On 29 April 1918 German occupation authorities, unhappy with the socialist Central Rada of the Ukrainian People's Republic, supported a coup by General Pavlo Skoropadsky. A congress of landowners proclaimed him hetman, reviving the title of the Cossack Hetmanate, and the state was renamed the Ukrainian State.
ukrainian-state.r: Skoropadsky ruled with broad powers and a cabinet of largely Russian-educated officials. He restored private property in land, angering peasants, and depended on German troops. Yet the state built a working administration and founded the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences, a national library and new universities in Kyiv and Kamianets-Podilskyi.
ukrainian-state.e: When Germany collapsed in November 1918, Skoropadsky declared federation with a future non-Bolshevik Russia. A revolt led by the Directorate gathered strength, and on 14 December 1918 he abdicated and fled to Germany. The Directorate restored the Ukrainian People's Republic.

utigurs.t: A Bulgar nomad people east of the Sea of Azov whom Justinian set against their kinsmen the Kutrigurs in the 6th century.
utigurs.o: The Utigurs appear in Byzantine sources in the early 6th century as one of the two main Bulgar or Hunnic groups of the Pontic steppe, living east of the Don and around the Sea of Azov, with the related Kutrigurs to the west. Procopius traces both to two brothers, sons of a Hunnic king.
utigurs.r: They were pastoral nomads led by chiefs, and Byzantium paid them subsidies to keep them as allies. In 551 and again after the Kutrigur raid on Constantinople in 559, Justinian persuaded their ruler Sandilch to attack the Kutrigurs, and the two peoples wore each other down in prolonged warfare.
utigurs.e: The Avars and then the Western Turkic Khaganate subdued the Utigurs, who were under Turkic rule by 576. They later joined Kubrat's Old Great Bulgaria together with the Onogurs and Kutrigurs, before the Khazars absorbed the region.

unelli.t: Gallic people of the Cotentin peninsula whose leader Viridovix headed a coalition against Caesar in 56 BCE.
unelli.o: The Unelli held the Cotentin in western Normandy. Caesar lists them among the Armorican peoples who submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE.
unelli.r: In 56 BCE their chief Viridovix commanded a large army of the Unelli, Lexovii, Aulerci Eburovices and others, showing how a war leader could unite several peoples.
unelli.e: Quintus Titurius Sabinus lured the coalition into attacking his fortified camp uphill and routed it, and the Unelli submitted. Under Rome their chief town moved from Crociatonum to Cosedia, renamed Constantia in late antiquity, the origin of Coutances and of the name Cotentin.

uyghur-khaganate.t: A Turkic steppe empire that made Manichaeism its state religion, built cities in Mongolia and rescued the Tang dynasty during the An Lushan rebellion.
uyghur-khaganate.o: The Uyghurs, a leading tribe of the Toquz Oghuz confederation, joined the Basmyls and Karluks to overthrow the Second Turkic Khaganate in 744. Their chief Qutlugh Bilge Kol Qaghan then turned on his allies, becoming master of the Mongolian steppe.
uyghur-khaganate.r: Bayanchur Khan built the walled capital Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon River. The Uyghurs helped the Tang recover Chang'an and Luoyang from An Lushan's rebels in 757, and won a lucrative trade of horses for silk. In 762 Bogu Qaghan adopted Manichaeism from Sogdian missionaries, making the Uyghurs the only state to adopt it officially. Sogdian scribes and merchants were influential at court.
uyghur-khaganate.e: Weakened by famine, epidemic and succession disputes, the khaganate fell in 840 when the Yenisei Kyrgyz Khaganate sacked Ordu-Baliq. Uyghur groups fled south-west, founding the Kingdom of Qocho and the Ganzhou Uyghur state, and later formed part of the Kara-Khanid Khanate.

united-provinces-of-new-granada.t: A federation of New Granada's provinces during the 'Foolish Fatherland', torn by civil war before the Spanish reconquest of 1816.
united-provinces-of-new-granada.o: After the revolutions of 1810, delegates of several provinces of the Viceroyalty of New Granada signed an Act of Federation in November 1811, creating the United Provinces of New Granada. Its congress sat at Tunja and was led by Camilo Torres. Cartagena declared absolute independence from Spain the same month.
united-provinces-of-new-granada.r: The federation left great power to the provinces and quarrelled with the centralist Free and Independent State of Cundinamarca, leading to civil war. Bolívar, a refugee from Venezuela, wrote his Cartagena Manifesto there in 1812 and led campaigns for the federation. In 1814 he captured Bogotá for the United Provinces, which then moved its government there.
united-provinces-of-new-granada.e: Pablo Morillo's royalist expedition besieged Cartagena in 1815, starving it into surrender, and took Bogotá in May 1816. Leaders such as Camilo Torres and the scientist Francisco José de Caldas were executed. The period is remembered as the Patria Boba, the Foolish Fatherland.

upper-aulaqi-sultanate.t: A sultanate of the Aulaqi tribes based at Nisab, one of the protected states in the hinterland of British Aden.
upper-aulaqi-sultanate.o: The Aulaqi tribes of the Shabwa region formed several states. The Upper Aulaqi Sultanate, based at Nisab, emerged as a distinct power by around 1800, alongside the Upper Aulaqi Sheikhdom and the Lower Aulaqi Sultanate.
upper-aulaqi-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled a large but thinly populated territory of wadis and highland plateaus, where the Aulaqi were known as formidable fighters, many serving abroad as soldiers. The sultanate entered British protection by treaty and formed part of the Aden Protectorate. It joined the Federation of South Arabia in the 1960s.
upper-aulaqi-sultanate.e: When the National Liberation Front took power in 1967, the sultanate was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

usdiae.t: People of south-eastern Ireland known only from Ptolemy's Geography, placed inland near the Brigantes and Coriondi.
usdiae.o: The Usdiae appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 in the south-east of Ireland, inland of the coastal Brigantes (Ireland) and Manapii and near the Coriondi, roughly in the region of modern Kilkenny, Carlow or Laois. As with all of Ptolemy's Irish names, the data came second-hand from earlier sea reports.
usdiae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or way of life, and no convincing link has been found between their name and any people of early Irish tradition. The fertile lands of the Barrow and Nore valleys in this region supported mixed farming and cattle-raising.
usdiae.e: The Usdiae do not appear again in any source. The region where Ptolemy placed them later belonged to the Kingdom of Osraige and the Kingdom of Leinster.

ukhaydirid-emirate.t: An Alid dynasty that ruled the oases of al-Yamama in central Arabia for nearly two centuries.
ukhaydirid-emirate.o: Around 866 Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Ukhaydir, a descendant of al-Hasan ibn Ali, fled the Hejaz after a failed revolt and took control of al-Yamama in Najd. He founded a dynasty with its seat at al-Khidrima, in the region of modern al-Kharj south of Riyadh.
ukhaydirid-emirate.r: The Ukhaydirids governed farming oases and the Bedouin tribes around them. Later sources describe them as Zaydi Shi'is. Their land lay on pilgrimage and trade routes between Iraq, Bahrain and the Hejaz, and the Persian traveller Nasir Khusraw, who passed in the 1050s, mentions a poor but fortified Alid emirate.
ukhaydirid-emirate.e: The rise of the Qarmatians of Bahrain to the east reduced the emirate to a client. It faded in the mid-11th century, with little recorded about its end, and al-Yamama fell under local tribal chiefs.

uyunid-emirate.t: An Arab dynasty of the Abd al-Qays tribe that ended Qarmatian rule in eastern Arabia and governed al-Ahsa and Qatif for nearly two centuries.
uyunid-emirate.o: In 1076 Abd Allah ibn Ali al-Uyuni, a chief of the Abd al-Qays tribe, rebelled against the Qarmatians of Bahrain. With the help of a Seljuk Empire army he took al-Ahsa in 1077 and founded an emirate covering the oases and coast of eastern Arabia and the Bahrain islands.
uyunid-emirate.r: Much of what is known comes from the poetry of Ibn al-Muqarrab, a member of the family, and its commentary. The emirate controlled the date groves of al-Ahsa and Qatif and the pearl banks around Awal, the main Bahrain island. It was weakened by family quarrels and lost the islands for a time to the Emirate of Kish.
uyunid-emirate.e: By the 13th century the Uyunids were reduced to a weak local power. Around 1253 the Usfurid dynasty of the Banu Amir took al-Ahsa and replaced them.

united-belgian-states.t: The first independent Belgian state, a confederation formed in the Brabant Revolution of 1789–1790 and modelled partly on the United States.
united-belgian-states.o: Joseph II's reforms of courts, church and administration angered the estates of the Austrian Netherlands. In 1789 exiles organised an army at Breda, defeated the Austrians at Turnhout in October, and by December drove them from most of the country. On 11 January 1790 the provinces declared independence as the United Belgian States.
united-belgian-states.r: The confederation's treaty created a sovereign congress in Brussels while leaving each province its old institutions. Power lay with the conservative Statists of Henri van der Noot, who defended traditional privileges and the Church, against the democratic Vonckists of Jean-François Vonck, who were driven into exile. No foreign power recognised the state.
united-belgian-states.e: Divided and without allies, the United Belgian States collapsed when Leopold II's Austrian army reoccupied the country in December 1790. The Austrian Netherlands was restored until the French conquest of 1794.

upper-yafa-sultanate.t: A loose sultanate of the upper Yafa highlands, one of the most independent of the British protectorate states of south Arabia.
upper-yafa-sultanate.o: Like its neighbour the Lower Yafa Sultanate, Upper Yafa emerged in the early 18th century when the Yafa tribes rejected rule by the Qasimid State. The sultans of the Harhara family, based at Mahjaba, held a loose primacy over the upper Yafa clans and their sheikhdoms.
upper-yafa-sultanate.r: Authority was weak and shared with several sheikhs, and the sultanate had almost no administration. Its rugged highlands were famous for their stone tower houses and terraces, and many of its men emigrated or served as soldiers in Hadramawt and India. Upper Yafa entered British protection late and stayed outside the Federation of South Arabia, remaining part of the Aden Protectorate.
upper-yafa-sultanate.e: In 1967, as British rule ended, the National Liberation Front took control and Upper Yafa was incorporated into South Yemen.

umbrians.t: Italic people of central Italy, called by Pliny the oldest in Italy, whose ritual Iguvine Tablets are the longest surviving text in any Italic language other than Latin.
umbrians.o: The Umbrians lived in the upper Tiber valley and the Apennines east of Etruria from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers believed they had once held a much larger area before being pushed back by Etruscans and Gauls. They spoke Umbrian, an Osco-Umbrian language.
umbrians.r: Umbrian communities were independent towns and hill sanctuaries, among them Iguvium, Tuder, Asisium, Mevania, Spoletium and Ameria, without a lasting central government. The Iguvine Tablets, seven bronze plates of the 3rd to 1st centuries BCE, set out the rituals of the Atiedian Brethren, a priestly college of Iguvium, giving rich detail on Italic religion. Bronze votive figures from mountain shrines are typical of their art.
umbrians.e: Rome founded Narnia in 299 BCE, and after the battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE, where some Umbrians backed the anti-Roman coalition, the Umbrian towns became allies. The last resistance, at Sarsina, ended in 266 BCE. They gained citizenship after the Social War, and the name survives in the Italian region of Umbria.

united-kingdom-of-the-netherlands.t: The kingdom created at the Congress of Vienna to unite the northern and southern Low Countries under William I, broken apart by the Belgian Revolution.
united-kingdom-of-the-netherlands.o: The Congress of Vienna joined the former Dutch Republic and the Austrian Netherlands into one kingdom as a barrier against France. William I, sovereign prince of the Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands, proclaimed himself king in March 1815, and Dutch and allied troops fought at Waterloo that June. He also became grand duke of Luxembourg.
united-kingdom-of-the-netherlands.r: William I ruled energetically, with the capital alternating between Brussels and The Hague. He founded universities at Ghent and Liège, the Société Générale bank and supported industry such as Cockerill's ironworks. But the south, more populous and largely Catholic and French-speaking among its elites, resented Dutch-dominated government, language policy and taxes.
united-kingdom-of-the-netherlands.e: After a riot at a Brussels opera performance in August 1830, the Belgian Revolution drove out Dutch troops and created the Kingdom of Belgium. William refused to accept this until the Treaty of London in 1839, which left the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the north.

ukrainian-ssr.t: Soviet Ukraine, the Soviet Union's second-largest republic, which suffered the Holodomor and the Second World War and became independent Ukraine in 1991.
ukrainian-ssr.o: After two earlier attempts, Bolshevik forces proclaimed a Ukrainian Socialist Soviet Republic in January 1919, with Kharkiv as capital. Despite defeats by the Whites and Poles, the Soviet regime was established by 1920, and in 1922 the republic became a founding member of the Soviet Union.
ukrainian-ssr.r: The 1920s brought Ukrainisation in schools and culture, but Stalin's forced collectivisation caused the famine of 1932 and 1933, the Holodomor, which killed millions. The capital moved to Kyiv in 1934. The republic gained western Ukraine in 1939, was devastated by German occupation, joined the United Nations in 1945 and received Crimea in 1954. Leaders such as Petro Shelest and Volodymyr Shcherbytsky ran it for Moscow.
ukrainian-ssr.e: The Chernobyl disaster in 1986 and the reforms of Gorbachev fed a national movement. On 24 August 1991 the Verkhovna Rada declared independence, confirmed by referendum on 1 December, and Leonid Kravchuk became the first president of independent Ukraine.

united-arab-emirates.t: A federation of seven emirates formed from the Trucial States in 1971, now a global hub of trade, finance and aviation.
united-arab-emirates.o: After Britain announced its withdrawal from the Gulf, Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi and Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum of Dubai led talks among the Trucial States. On 2 December 1971 six sheikhdoms formed the United Arab Emirates; the Sheikhdom of Ras al-Khaimah joined in February 1972. Bahrain and Qatar chose separate independence.
united-arab-emirates.r: The Federal Supreme Council of the seven rulers elects the president, traditionally the ruler of Abu Dhabi, while each emirate keeps control of its own resources. Abu Dhabi's oil funds the federation, and Dubai built a trading, tourism and aviation economy around Jebel Ali port and Emirates airline. Foreign residents make up nearly nine tenths of the population.
united-arab-emirates.e: Zayed was president until his death in 2004, followed by Khalifa bin Zayed and in 2022 Mohamed bin Zayed. The UAE has become an active regional power and normalised relations with Israel in 2020.

united-states-of-the-ionian-islands.t: British protectorate over the seven Ionian Islands from 1815 to 1864, whose cession to Greece was the first enlargement of the Greek kingdom.
united-states-of-the-ionian-islands.o: After Napoleon's fall, the Treaty of Paris in November 1815 made the Ionian Islands, formerly the French Ionian Islands and earlier the Septinsular Republic, a nominally independent state under the exclusive protection of Britain. Corfu, the last French-held island, had been handed over in 1814.
united-states-of-the-ionian-islands.r: Real power lay with the British Lord High Commissioner. The first, Sir Thomas Maitland, nicknamed King Tom, imposed the constitution of 1817, which left an island assembly and senate with little authority. The British built roads, aqueducts and the Ionian Academy, but many islanders resented their rule. From the 1840s Radical politicians demanded union with Greece, and their assembly voted for it repeatedly.
united-states-of-the-ionian-islands.e: After the Greeks deposed King Otto, Britain agreed to cede the islands to encourage the new King George I. Under the Treaty of London the islands joined the Kingdom of Greece in 1864, and Corfu's fortifications were partly demolished.

upi.t: Upi, the Late Bronze Age territory of Damascus, the southernmost Syrian land held by Egypt and a frontier with the Hittites.
upi.o: Upi, or Apa, was the oasis of Damascus and the land around it. It came under the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom after the campaigns of Thutmose III in the 15th century BCE, forming one of Egypt's provinces in Syria.
upi.r: In the Amarna letters, the local ruler Biryawaza acted as Egypt's agent, defending the area against the Hittites and their allies such as Aitakkama of Kadesh. Damascus served as a base for Egyptian officials and troops.
upi.e: Upi remained the Egyptian border district after the Battle of Kadesh and the peace treaty of Ramesses II and Hattusili III c. 1259 BCE. With the collapse of Egyptian power after 1200 BCE, Damascus later rose again as the capital of Aram-Damascus.

ubangi-shari.t: The French colony on the Ubangi River that became the Central African Republic, exploited by concession companies.
ubangi-shari.o: French posts along the Ubangi River, including Bangui founded in 1889, were organised in 1903 into the colony of Ubangi-Shari, separate from Gabon and Middle Congo. Chad was attached to it for some years. It formed part of French Equatorial Africa from 1910.
ubangi-shari.r: Concession companies forced people to collect rubber and later grow cotton, and thousands were conscripted to build the Congo-Ocean railway in Middle Congo. The Kongo-Wara rebellion of the Gbaya from 1928 to 1931 was one of the largest colonial-era revolts. Sultanates such as Dar al Kuti, Bangassou and Zemio were absorbed into the administration.
ubangi-shari.e: After 1946 the Catholic priest Barthélemy Boganda led the nationalist movement. Ubangi-Shari became the Central African Republic in December 1958 and independent on 13 August 1960, after Boganda's death in an air crash in 1959.

united-duchies-of-julich-cleves-berg.t: A union of Lower Rhine duchies formed in 1521 whose succession crisis of 1609 brought Europe to the brink of war.
united-duchies-of-julich-cleves-berg.o: John III of Cleves-Mark married Maria, heiress of Jülich, Berg and Ravensberg. On his father-in-law's death in 1511 and his own father's in 1521, he united the Duchy of Jülich, the Duchy of Cleves and the Duchy of Berg with the counties of Mark and Ravensberg, ruling from Düsseldorf.
united-duchies-of-julich-cleves-berg.r: John III and his adviser Konrad von Heresbach pursued a moderate, Erasmian church policy. The duchies were rich in textiles, iron and Rhine trade, and the court was a centre of humanism. John's daughter Anne of Cleves married Henry VIII of England in 1540, and his son William the Rich lost Guelders to Charles V in 1543.
united-duchies-of-julich-cleves-berg.e: The mentally ill Duke John William died childless in 1609, setting off the War of the Jülich Succession between Brandenburg and Palatinate-Neuburg. The Treaty of Xanten in 1614 divided the lands: Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg went to Brandenburg, and Jülich and Berg to Palatinate-Neuburg.

ui-chennselaig.t: Ruling dynasty of south Leinster, based at Ferns, that produced Diarmait Mac Murchada, whose alliance with the Anglo-Normans changed Irish history.
ui-chennselaig.o: The Uí Chennselaig, 'descendants of Énna Cennselach', emerged in the 5th and 6th centuries as the leading dynasty of southern Leinster, in modern Wexford and Carlow. Their royal centre and church were at Ferns, founded by St Máedóc. They competed with the Uí Dúnlainge of the north for the kingship of the Kingdom of Leinster.
ui-chennselaig.r: Brandub mac Echach, who defeated the high king at Dún Bolg in 598, was their most famous early king. After a long period of northern dominance, Diarmait mac Máel na mBó revived their fortunes in the 11th century, taking Dublin and ruling much of southern Ireland. The family of his descendants, the Meic Murchada or MacMurroughs, became the kings of Leinster.
ui-chennselaig.e: Diarmait Mac Murchada, driven out in 1166, brought Anglo-Norman knights to Ireland. On his death in 1171 Strongbow took Leinster. The MacMurrough Kavanaghs later revived as independent lords in Wexford and Carlow, resisting English rule until the 16th century.
